response.title: What's a good first 3D printer for making strong working parts for the garage and car, not toys, for under $1,000?
response.answer:
For making strong, functional garage and automotive parts under $1,000, I'd prioritize an enclosed 3D printer that handles engineering-grade materials reliably, rather than one that simply prints fast or produces pretty models.

My top choice would be a Bambu Lab P1S, with the QIDI Plus4 worth serious consideration if you're planning to make parts exposed to engine-bay temperatures.

The important distinction is what you can print with it. For brackets, tool holders, clips, jigs, housings, and replacement plastic components, material choice often matters more than the printer itself.

The printers I'd consider
Shop
Best for engineering parts

QIDI Plus5

$749.00

at Best Buy

Actively heated chamber, large 320 × 320 × 300 mm build area, and support for demanding materials. This is where I'd put my money for automotive projects.

View printer

Shop

Bambu Lab P2S

$450–$650 approx.

Excellent beginner-friendly alternative. Better choice if you want less setup and troubleshooting. Smaller build volume and no independently heated chamber.

A very good all-rounder for PETG, ASA, and many functional parts.

Bambu Lab P1S 3D Printer

$449.99

at Hillwave Networks

Proven, easy-to-use machine. Great for general garage parts, but carbon-fiber-filled materials require hardware upgrades, and it lacks active chamber heating.

View printer

The QIDI Plus5 is the successor to the Plus4, which was independently praised for its engineering-material performance. 
Tom's Hardware
+1

Materials matter more than you might think

Material

	

Best use




PETG

	

Garage organizers, brackets, tool fixtures, general-purpose parts




ASA

	

Exterior car clips, covers, weather-resistant parts




PA-CF (carbon-fiber nylon)

	

Stiff, strong brackets, housings, functional components




PC / PC blends

	

Heat-resistant, rigid parts where the specific grade is suitable




TPU

	

Flexible pads, protective covers, vibration dampers

A caution: carbon-fiber-filled nylon is stiff, but it isn't automatically stronger in every direction. Layer adhesion, moisture control, print orientation, and part design are crucial.

For car work, I would not use ordinary hobby-printed parts for brakes, steering, suspension, seat belts, or other safety-critical components. Engine-bay parts also need temperature and chemical-resistance checks.

How I'd spend your $1,000

Before tax and shipping. Ventilation may require additional spending; ASA, ABS, and other engineering filaments should not be printed in an unventilated occupied space.

I would skip multi-color accessories and spend the money on a filament dryer, good materials, and ventilation.

One question that would change my recommendation: What kinds of car parts are you hoping to make?

Under-hood parts — brackets, ducts, mounts, clips
Interior parts — trim, switches, consoles, adapters

A mix of everything
